title: Climate-dependent trade-offs between direct and indirect coupling in photovoltaic hydrogen production
content: Renewable-powered water electrolysis requires efficient coupling between intermittent electricity generation and electrolyzer operation, yet how climatic conditions determine the optimal electrical architecture remains unclear because direct coupling avoids conversion losses, whereas indirect coupling adds power-electronic costs and losses. Here, we develop a climate-resolved framework to reveal how meteorological variability governs the trade-off between photovoltaic (PV) operating-point mismatch and power-conditioning losses in PV-water electrolysis systems. By coupling dynamic PV, power-electronic, and electrolyzer models, we identify temperature-driven voltage decoupling as a dominant limitation of direct coupling: as temperature decreases, the PV maximum-power-point voltage increases substantially, while the PV–electrolyzer intersection voltage changes little, resulting in power losses of up to 18.35% at −30 °C. In contrast, indirect coupling using incremental conductance maximum power point tracking (INC-MPPT) achieves sub-second tracking with conversion losses below 2.98%, enabling improved annual hydrogen production. Across six representative climate regions and 163 photovoltaic plant sites in China, indirect coupling increases annual hydrogen production by up to 7.95% and reduces energy losses from 9.66% to 2.08% in highly variable cold climates, while direct coupling remains economically competitive in stable low-latitude regions because of its lower system complexity. Techno-economic analysis further identifies climate-dependent regions where either coupling strategy becomes economically favorable, revealing a near-cost-parity zone where both architectures remain competitive. By integrating dynamic performance with techno-economic analysis, this work establishes climate as a critical design variable for selecting PV–electrolyzer coupling architectures and provides a quantitative basis for climate-adaptive renewable hydrogen deployment.
